claims.text: Rapid thermal quenching induces retained short-range chemical ordering that dominates phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Quench-induced short-range order preserves a single-phase solid solution against competing intermetallic or sigma phases.
Short-range order suppresses diffusion-mediated secondary-phase formation.
Secondary phases formed during cooling would lower high-temperature strength.
Secondary phases formed during cooling would lower cryogenic toughness.
High-temperature homogenization of arc-melted Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni can produce a uniform high-temperature single-phase solid solution.
Whether the homogenized alloy is FCC, BCC, or mixed depends on its Al content.
Rapid quenching and cooling at approximately 1°C/min produce different degrees of retained short-range order.
Retained short-range order and local atomic distortions alter the free-energy landscape between the single-phase state and secondary phases.
Rapid quenching freezes in high chemical disorder together with localized short-range order.
Quenched-in localized short-range order kinetically hinders diffusion-driven ordered-intermetallic precipitation.
Suppressing diffusion and precipitation maintains a single-phase architecture.
A single-phase architecture is crucial for simultaneously retaining high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
The rapidly quenched alloy will retain a larger single-phase fraction than the slow-cooled baseline.
The rapidly quenched alloy will have greater high-temperature mechanical strength than the slow-cooled alloy.
The rapidly quenched alloy will have greater cryogenic toughness than the slow-cooled alloy.
The rapidly quenched alloy will maintain resistance to environmental degradation relative to the slow-cooled alloy.
The rapidly quenched alloy will maintain resistance to radiation-induced damage relative to the slow-cooled alloy.
Conventional slow cooling permits sufficient atomic diffusion for intermetallic or sigma-phase precipitation to begin.
Cooling rate is the dominant variable governing atomic diffusion and phase stability within the stated boundary.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as a single-phase solid solution but parenthetically as potentially 'FCC or BCC mixed'; an FCC+BCC mixture would not be single phase.

The hypothesis attributes stability to a high degree of quench-induced short-range order, whereas the mechanism emphasizes quenching in high chemical disorder with only localized short-range order. These can coexist, but the direction and identity of the proposed mediator are not stated consistently.
